name: Nikhil Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, government or political parties, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential; may I ask you about an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Nikhil Usman, 43, and I do general carpentry on building sites. I live with my partner and our two school-age children, and most months the mortgage takes a big bite.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like, from arriving on site to going home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I usually meet the crew by the site gate at seven, carry timber in, measure openings and help cut boards. I am still learning, so the foreman checks my measurements; I like seeing a room take shape, but my back is tired by the ride home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the foreman that anything which gets the material list right is useful. I would also say our hours should not be shortened just because one office task got quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small software change will not cut the boards for me. My work is mostly measuring, cutting and carrying, but the mortgage still worries me when a week has fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reporting to the current site and ask the foreman about next week before I leave on Friday. After a short week, I would pause household purchases we can manage without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small change itself sounds manageable because my day is mostly physical. The thinner part is our savings; one missed day makes me check the bank balance again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many days did you work last week, and what would one day without pay change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had five days last week and four the week before. That missing day meant we delayed replacing a worn pair of school shoes until payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound steady about AI but worried about the bills; which part stays with you tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bill dates stay in my head more than the software story. I sit with my partner after the children are asleep and check which pay has cleared.

say: I would tell the foreman that **a correct list** is useful.
I would say **our hours should stay** if one office task gets quicker.
think: I do not expect **small software changes** to replace my hands-on tasks.
I have **thin savings**, so a quiet week remains difficult.
do: Keep reporting to the **current site** and ask about next week’s shifts before Friday.
Pause **optional purchases** after a short week to leave more room for bills.
feel: **Small changes** feel manageable, but irregular shifts still make me check our balance.
S0.quote: A small software change will not cut the boards for me.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **small office changes** from the hands-on work he does each day.
**A short week** presses on the household even with little direct AI change.

steps.text: Keep reporting to the current site and ask about next week’s shifts
Pause optional household purchases after a short week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software may help the office send a cleaner material list. On site, someone still has to check that the delivery matches the room we are building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An order changing on a screen does not tell me whether a builder has booked a whole project. I could lose hours if work dries up, but there is no reason to assume fewer office staff automatically means fewer site projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to show me the AI ordering screen while I am paid, one delivery at a time. I would keep doing the carpentry jobs I already have until someone gives me a real reason to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than frightened by a screen I have not used yet. The worry is that I cannot afford to practise on my own time if the site gets quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which task on your current site might change first if the office uses more AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The material list and delivery slot are the parts I see coming from the office. I would want to compare the AI list with the actual opening sizes before timber is unloaded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training yourself, or what would make you try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not borrow for an evening course while the mortgage is tight. Letting me use the ordering screen during paid hours would give me a fair chance to learn it.

say: I would say **software may help** the office send a cleaner material list.
I would say someone on site must **check the delivery** against the room.
think: I cannot tell whether an **order change** means a builder booked a whole project.
**My hours** could shrink if site work dries up, though fewer office staff do not prove fewer projects.
do: Learn the **AI ordering screen** with the foreman during paid hours, one delivery at a time.
Keep doing the **assigned carpentry** while work remains available.
feel: I feel watchful because I cannot afford **unpaid practice** if site work becomes quiet.
S1.quote: An order changing on a screen does not tell me whether a builder has booked a whole project.
fieldNote: He does not assume office automation removes **a whole construction project** or a site job.
**Paid practice** is his condition for learning a new tool without risking household money.

steps.text: Learn the AI ordering screen with the foreman during paid hours
Keep taking the carpentry shifts already assigned while available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a robot is not on our site today, and a room still needs timber cut and fitted. I would not tell the crew that this means our jobs are safe, because the card says thinking AI comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI could do the measuring notes and quotes that I sometimes help prepare, so I cannot count on that part of my work after 2028. My hands-on tasks may continue for a while, but the later robot date does not promise me shifts until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask the foreman to let me practise fitting interior doors and checking my own measurements. In 2029, I would keep asking for paid site tasks and put a small amount aside only in a full-pay week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels like a short time to learn enough for steadier work. I can make a plan, but I still have to earn each month and I cannot buy a promise of future shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children if your hours were cut in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them we may need to skip the seaside trip that year. I would explain that their school things come first and that the change is not their fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You see a delay before robots but cannot count on shifts; how would you use that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman which practical tasks are coming up rather than assume he can keep me on. If he has no work, I would ask two builders nearby whether they need a junior hand, without pretending a vacancy is certain.

say: I would say **thinking AI comes first**, with robots three years later.
I would not call **my site job safe** just because I use my hands.
think: I think **AI could take** the measuring notes and quotes I sometimes help prepare after 2028.
I think my **hands-on tasks** may continue for a while, but that does not guarantee shifts before robots arrive.
do: Practise **fitting doors** and checking measurements with the foreman before 2028.
Keep asking for **paid site tasks** in 2029 and save a small amount only in a full-pay week.
feel: **Two years** feels short for learning enough to find steadier work.
I can plan, but I still need **monthly wages** and cannot buy a promise of future shifts.
S2.quote: My hands-on tasks may continue for a while, but the later robot date does not promise me shifts until then.
fieldNote: **Exposed tasks** include the measuring notes and quotes, rather than every part of carpentry.
The **2029 plan** uses paid practice and cautious saving while leaving future shifts uncertain.

steps.text: Practise fitting interior doors with the foreman before 2028
In 2029, save a small amount only in a full-pay week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives a crew more time to practise than two years does. I would also say nobody should promise that the building trade will keep every worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, AI may take the measuring notes, quotes and schedules I sometimes help with. I would still need a builder to choose me for paid practical work, and I do not know how many nearby jobs there will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask each winter to learn one task I do not yet do well, starting with fitting doors properly. In 2032, I would look at the work actually offered before deciding whether a paid certificate is worth the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use five years to learn a proper door fit, one paid job at a time. It is still uncomfortable because one mistake with our small cushion could leave us behind on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which new task would you ask to learn first, and from whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to let me hang an interior door while he checks the frame and my measurements. I have made a gap uneven before, so I know exactly what he would need to correct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide that a paid course is worth the cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local builder would need to say the certificate is used for real work they expect to hire for. If nobody can tell me that, I will not borrow money just to have paper in a drawer.

say: I would say **five years** gives a crew more time to practise than two years.
I would add that nobody should promise a **permanent job** in the trade.
think: I think **AI may take** the measuring notes, quotes and schedules I sometimes help with by 2031.
I need **paid practical work**, which depends on a builder choosing me and openings nearby.
do: Ask each winter to learn a **new carpentry task**, starting with fitting doors.
Check in 2032 whether **local work** is available before deciding on a paid certificate.
feel: **The extra time** lets me learn a proper door fit, one paid job at a time.
Our **small cushion** makes a costly mistake feel serious because of the mortgage.
S3.quote: I can use five years to learn a proper door fit, one paid job at a time.
fieldNote: **Extra time** gives him a practical way to improve without assuming permanent security.
The **2032 choice** depends on actual local work before he risks money on a certificate.

steps.text: Ask each winter to learn another paid carpentry task before 2031
In 2032, check local work before deciding on a paid certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives my family time to plan, but it does not promise me work after 2039. I would say that out loud at the site because people should not hear “later” as “never”.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036, the computer-based notes and planning I sometimes do could be gone. The robots come later, but my children will be much older by 2039 and our household costs may change in ways I cannot know now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep building practical skill through paid site tasks while there is work to learn from. In 2037, I would talk with my partner and our older child about study choices when the child is actually making them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning gives me time to notice what builders are asking people to do. It does not make me calm about the mortgage, because there is no guarantee my work lasts until the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what your children study now because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not steer them now toward a job that may also change. When our older child chooses subjects, we can look at the actual options and talk it through together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can ask for practice across several winters and see which building tasks are still offered. I would still need to make the next mortgage payment each month while that picture becomes clearer.

say: I would say **ten years** gives my family time to plan, but it does not promise me work after 2039.
I would say “later” does not mean **never** at the site.
think: I expect **computer-based notes** I sometimes do could be gone by 2036.
**My children** will be much older by 2039 and household costs may change in ways I cannot know now.
do: Keep building **practical skills** through paid site tasks while work is available.
Talk with my partner and older child about **study choices** in 2037 when the child is making them.
feel: **The warning** gives time to notice which tasks builders still offer.
Our **mortgage worries me** because no one guarantees work until robots arrive.
S4.quote: Ten years gives my family time to plan, but it does not promise me work after 2039.
fieldNote: He values the **longer warning** but does not confuse delayed robots with permanent protection.
He postpones education decisions until his older child faces **real subject choices**.

steps.text: Keep learning practical carpentry through paid site tasks as offered
Agree with partner to revisit older child’s study choices when subjects are chosen

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two years is hardly time to build a cushion. Paid practice with the foreman and steady shifts would help more than a course I have to borrow for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People talk about a trade as if it is one skill, but I am still learning the basics and need someone to give me a chance. My partner and I check every week’s pay because the mortgage does not wait for a promise.

headlineQuote: My partner and I check every week’s pay because the mortgage does not wait for a promise.
portrait: Nikhil is a **43-year-old junior carpenter** supporting his partner and two school-age children.
His **thin savings** make missed shifts more urgent than modest software changes.
He is **slow to adopt technology** and prefers paid practice on a live site.
He sees **later robot risk**, not a guarantee that carpentry will stay secure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him because two years is too little time to build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** with the foreman and steady shifts would help more than debt-financed training.
